articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Pensacola's $280 Million Question: Where the City Plans to Spend Your Money Next Year
articles.dek: The proposed FY2027 budget lands before council next month. A breakdown of what's in it, what's missing, and which neighborhoods get left out.
brief: Mayor's proposed $280.4 million FY2027 budget increases spending 6.2% over current year
Police and fire departments claim 42% of general fund; stormwater infrastructure gets $18.7 million boost
West Pensacola neighborhoods see minimal capital improvement funding for third consecutive year
articles.body:
The binder lands on the table with a thud. Three hundred and twelve pages of line items, department requests, and capital improvement schedules. City Council members have six weeks to digest it before the first budget workshop in late June.

Mayor D.C. Reeves released the proposed fiscal year 2027 budget last Thursday, a $280.4 million spending plan that would take effect October 1. The document represents a 6.2% increase over the current year's $264.1 million budget and relies on projected property tax revenues that assume continued growth in the local real estate market.

"This budget reflects our commitment to public safety and infrastructure while maintaining fiscal responsibility," Reeves said at a press conference Friday morning. "We're investing in the services residents depend on."

What that investment looks like depends largely on where you live.

The Big Numbers

The general fund—the city's main operating account—would grow to $142.3 million, up from $131.8 million in FY2026. Property taxes contribute the largest share at $58.2 million, followed by sales tax revenue at $34.7 million and utility franchise fees at $19.1 million.

The proposed millage rate holds steady at 4.1193 mills. But because property values have risen an average of 8.3% countywide according to the Escambia County Property Appraiser's preliminary estimates, most homeowners will see higher tax bills even without a rate increase. A home valued at $250,000 last year that's now assessed at $270,750 would pay roughly $83 more in city taxes.

Public safety dominates the general fund. The Pensacola Police Department's proposed allocation of $38.4 million represents a 7.1% increase, driven largely by a new officer recruitment initiative and retention bonuses designed to address staffing shortages. The department currently operates with 287 sworn officers against an authorized strength of 312.

The Pensacola Fire Department would receive $21.3 million, including funds for a new ladder truck at Station 4 on North Palafox Street. Combined, police and fire account for 42% of general fund spending.

Where the Capital Goes

The capital improvement plan tells a different story than the operating budget. Of the $47.8 million earmarked for infrastructure projects, nearly 40% flows to two initiatives: the Maritime Park area redevelopment and stormwater system upgrades.

The stormwater allocation—$18.7 million spread across multiple projects—addresses some of the city's most persistent flooding problems. The Cervantes Street corridor from A Street to Alcaniz Street is slated for a complete drainage overhaul, a project that's been on planning documents since 2019. The Bayou Texar outfall improvements, delayed twice due to permitting issues with the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, finally appear with full funding.

"We've been waiting on Cervantes for years," said District 6 Council member Allison Patton at Thursday's council meeting. "My constituents are tired of their cars floating every time we get two inches of rain."

The Maritime Park area continues to absorb significant city investment. The proposed budget includes $8.4 million for public infrastructure supporting the Studer Properties mixed-use development, including a new parking structure, streetscaping, and utility connections. The city argues these investments will generate tax revenue and economic activity. Critics point out the public is subsidizing private development in an already thriving downtown while other neighborhoods wait.

The Gaps

Council member Teniadé Broughton represents District 7, which includes portions of West Pensacola that have seen minimal capital improvement funding for three consecutive budget cycles. Her district contains some of the city's oldest infrastructure—water mains dating to the 1950s, streets without sidewalks, and parks that haven't been updated since the Reagan administration.

"Every year I ask the same question," Broughton said. "When does west of I-110 become a priority?"

The proposed budget allocates $2.1 million for District 7 capital projects, compared to $11.3 million for District 2 in the downtown and East Hill areas. City officials note that some infrastructure funding flows through county and state programs not reflected in the municipal budget, but the disparity remains stark.

The West Pensacola Recreation Center, built in 1978 and last renovated in 2003, is not included in the capital plan. Neither is the long-discussed extension of the Pensacola Bay Trail westward past its current terminus at Bayfront Parkway.

Parks and recreation overall receives $6.2 million in the capital budget, with the majority directed toward Bayview Park improvements and a new restroom facility at Sanders Beach. The department's operating budget would hold essentially flat at $8.9 million—a cut in real terms once inflation is factored in.

What Happens Next

Council members will hold their first budget workshop on June 24, with additional sessions scheduled through July. Public hearings are set for September 10 and September 24, with final adoption required before the new fiscal year begins October 1.

The budget document is available on the city's website, though navigating its 312 pages requires patience. Summary dashboards that previous administrations provided have not been updated since FY2024.

Council member Jennifer Brahier, who chairs the budget committee, said she plans to request detailed breakdowns of several line items before the first workshop.

"There are numbers in here that don't match what departments told us during strategic planning," Brahier said. "We need explanations before we can evaluate this responsibly."

The mayor's office did not respond to a request for comment on specific discrepancies Brahier identified.

Residents who wish to comment on the proposed budget can attend the public hearings or submit written comments to the city clerk's office. The deadline for written submissions is September 17.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: Pensacola Beach Lost 40 Feet of Dune This Winter. The Fix Will Cost Millions Nobody Has.
articles.dek: Santa Rosa Island Authority officials say federal renourishment funds won't arrive until 2028 at earliest. Property owners are getting nervous.
brief: Winter storms stripped an average of 40 feet from Pensacola Beach's protective dune system, with some sections losing over 60 feet
The Army Corps of Engineers estimates a full renourishment project would cost $48 million, but federal funding is not expected until 2028 at earliest
Santa Rosa Island Authority is exploring emergency measures including temporary sand fencing and a potential local taxing district to bridge the gap
articles.body:
Stand at the public walkover at Casino Beach and look east. The dune line that protected the parking lot last September is gone. What remains is a ragged escarpment, six feet of vertical sand face carved by five months of persistent northeast swells.

Paolo Ghio measured it himself in early May. The Santa Rosa Island Authority's director of developmental services has been walking the beach with a GPS unit and a growing sense of dread since February.

"We lost forty feet on average," Ghio told the SRIA board at its May 14 meeting. "Some sections between Portofino and Avenida 23, we're looking at sixty-plus feet gone. That's not erosion. That's amputation."

A Winter Unlike Others

Pensacola Beach loses sand every winter. The process is predictable: cold fronts push waves from the north and northwest, pulling sand offshore into sandbars that typically migrate back during calmer summer months. Engineers call this the seasonal envelope. The beach breathes in and out.

This year the beach only exhaled.

Between November 2025 and March 2026, seventeen significant weather systems crossed the Gulf of Mexico with sustained onshore winds. The National Weather Service recorded 23 days with wave heights exceeding six feet at the Pensacola Pass buoy. The ten-year average is nine days.

"We never got a recovery window," said Dr. Phillip Hartley, a coastal geologist at the University of West Florida who has studied Santa Rosa Island for two decades. "Every time the beach started rebuilding, another system would knock it back. The cumulative effect is what you see now."

What you see now are swimming pools perched on exposed pilings. PVC drain pipes dangling in midair. Wooden walkovers that end abruptly at six-foot drops. Along the eastern reaches of the developed beach, some structures permitted with 200-foot setbacks from the dune line in the 1990s now sit less than 80 feet from the water at high tide.

The Money Problem

The solution is straightforward in concept: pump sand back onto the beach. The execution is neither simple nor cheap.

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers maintains Pensacola Beach as part of its coastal storm damage reduction program. The last major renourishment occurred in 2016 following Hurricane Ivan's lingering effects, placing 3.2 million cubic yards of sand along 7.5 miles of shoreline at a cost of $32 million. The federal government covered 65 percent. Escambia County and the SRIA split the rest.

Corps officials estimate the current damage would require a similar volume of sand. But costs have increased. Fuel prices. Dredging equipment availability. Environmental permitting. The current estimate sits at $48 million.

"The project is in our work plan," said Marcus Webb, a project manager with the Corps' Mobile District, in a phone interview. "But we're funded through congressional appropriations on a priority basis. Pensacola Beach is competing with projects across the entire Gulf and Atlantic coasts."

The earliest realistic construction window, Webb said, is summer 2028. Possibly 2029.

Three more winters away.

Property Owners Sound Alarms

Thomas Fitzgerald bought his three-bedroom unit at Regency Towers in 2019 for $485,000. He attends SRIA meetings now. He's never attended a government meeting in his life before this spring.

"I'm not a beach expert," Fitzgerald said after the May 14 session. "But I can see what's happening outside my window. Every week there's less beach. At some point my condo association is going to get an engineer's letter saying the building isn't safe. Then what?"

Fitzgerald is not alone. The SRIA's May meeting drew 34 members of the public, nearly triple the typical attendance. Most were property owners. Most asked variations of the same question: What is being done?

Board chair Thomas Campanella acknowledged the frustration but offered no immediate remedies.

"We don't control federal appropriations," Campanella said. "We don't control the weather. What we control is this island's lease revenue and a limited ability to partner with the county on emergency measures."

Those emergency measures, Ghio explained, include deploying sand fencing to capture windblown sand and potentially trucking in material from upland sources to rebuild the most critical dune sections. Cost estimate: $2.3 million for a temporary fix that might last one or two seasons.

The SRIA's annual operating budget is approximately $7 million, most of it committed to infrastructure maintenance, public safety and debt service.

The Taxing District Question

One option has surfaced repeatedly in recent meetings: creating a Municipal Service Taxing Unit specifically for beach renourishment. Such a district would allow property owners on Santa Rosa Island to tax themselves for coastal protection projects, independent of county or federal funding cycles.

Escambia County Administrator Wes Moreno confirmed his office has received preliminary inquiries from SRIA staff about the mechanism.

"It's legally possible," Moreno said. "The county commission would have to approve it. The property owners within the proposed district would have to approve it. And someone would have to determine what the millage rate would need to be to generate meaningful revenue."

Back-of-envelope math is not encouraging. The SRIA estimates taxable property value on the island at roughly $1.8 billion. A one-mill levy would generate approximately $1.8 million annually—enough for Ghio's temporary sand fencing, not enough to fund a major renourishment project without decades of accumulation or significant borrowing.

A ten-mill levy would generate real money but would add roughly $2,500 in annual taxes to a median-value beach property. Political appetite for such an increase is unclear.

"Nobody wants to pay more taxes," said Pensacola Beach resident and frequent SRIA commenter Janet Morrison. "But nobody wants to watch their property fall into the Gulf either. At some point you have to choose."

What Happens Next

The SRIA board voted unanimously on May 14 to direct staff to pursue three parallel tracks: formal engagement with the Corps to accelerate the federal timeline, coordination with Escambia County on emergency stopgap measures, and development of a detailed proposal for a beach-specific taxing district to present to property owners by September.

Whether any of these efforts will outpace the next hurricane season remains uncertain.

Dr. Hartley, the UWF geologist, offered a blunt assessment.

"Santa Rosa Island has always been a dynamic system," he said. "It migrates. It changes. We've built a tremendous amount of fixed infrastructure on something that isn't fixed. The question isn't whether we'll keep fighting that battle. The question is how much we're willing to spend, and whether the money will be there when we need it."

Ghio walked the beach again last week. The GPS unit showed another three feet of loss near Casino Beach since his May measurements.

Summer hasn't officially started yet. Neither have the hurricanes.

articles.label: NAS Pensacola
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 100,000 Visitors and One Big Traffic Experiment
articles.dek: The city is testing a new shuttle system from downtown to the beach for this year's air show. Early signs suggest it might actually work.
brief: Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show expects 100,000 visitors over the weekend at NAS Pensacola
New shuttle system running from downtown parking garages to the base aims to ease traffic congestion
Friday practice runs saw 2,400 riders use the shuttle with wait times averaging under 12 minutes
articles.body:
The line at the Jefferson Street parking garage stretched around the corner at 9:47 a.m. Saturday. Families in lawn chairs. Coolers on wheels. Kids in Navy flight suits two sizes too big. They weren't waiting for their cars. They were waiting for a bus.

This is the scene Pensacola city officials have been hoping for since they announced the Blue Angels Homecoming Shuttle Program in February. The $340,000 pilot project represents the city's most ambitious attempt yet to solve the annual puzzle of moving 100,000 people to a naval air station built for 12,000.

"We've been talking about this for years," said Marcus Webb, Pensacola's public works director, standing near the shuttle staging area Friday morning. "This is the year we actually did it."

The Traffic Problem

Anyone who's tried to reach NAS Pensacola during homecoming week knows the math doesn't work. The base has parking for roughly 8,000 vehicles. The air show draws crowds that dwarf the population of most Escambia County towns. The result, historically, has been hours-long backups on Navy Boulevard and Blue Angel Parkway, frustrated residents in Warrington who can't leave their neighborhoods, and a small percentage of visitors who simply give up and turn around.

Last year, the Escambia County Sheriff's Office estimated vehicles sat in traffic for an average of 2 hours and 14 minutes on Saturday afternoon. Some didn't reach the gate until well after the show ended.

The shuttle program aims to intercept visitors before they ever head west. Three downtown parking garages—Jefferson Street, Palafox, and the new Romana Street structure—have been designated as staging areas. Buses run every eight minutes to the base, with dedicated lanes on portions of Navy Boulevard.

Early Numbers

Friday's practice show served as the real test. City officials released ridership numbers Saturday morning: 2,437 passengers used the shuttle system, with an average wait time of 11 minutes and an average trip time of 24 minutes.

For comparison, visitors who drove directly to the base Friday reported travel times ranging from 45 minutes to nearly two hours from downtown.

"We had people thanking drivers when they got off the bus," said Teresa Morales, operations manager for Escambia County Area Transit, which is running the shuttle fleet. "That doesn't usually happen."

The system isn't free. Riders pay $15 per person round-trip, with children under 5 free. Parking in the downtown garages costs an additional $10 flat rate. A family of four would spend $70 before they bought a single corn dog.

City officials defended the pricing at a press conference Thursday. "This isn't meant to be the only option," Webb said. "It's meant to be a better option for people who value their time."

What's Different This Year

The shuttle program emerged from a joint task force convened last August after the 2025 homecoming traffic debacle. That year, a fender bender at the Navy Boulevard and Fairfield Drive intersection created a cascade that essentially shut down westbound traffic for three hours. Social media filled with photos of families eating picnic lunches on the shoulder of the road.

Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes the Warrington area, had been vocal about finding solutions. He sits on the task force.

"My constituents can't get to the grocery store during homecoming," Bergosh said in September. "We love the Blue Angels. We're proud they're here. But we have to figure out how to share the roads."

The shuttle program is one piece. The task force also recommended staggered gate opening times, expanded park-and-ride lots at the Pensacola Interstate Fairgrounds, and a real-time traffic monitoring system that will push alerts to drivers' phones.

The fairgrounds lot opened at 7 a.m. Saturday and was full by 8:30. The alert system, developed in partnership with the Florida Department of Transportation, sent its first congestion warnings around 9:15 a.m.

Inside the Base

The Blue Angels homecoming show remains the largest annual event in Northwest Florida. The Navy estimates this year's crowd at between 95,000 and 110,000 over the two-day weekend. The practice show Friday drew roughly 35,000.

The gates opened at 8 a.m. Saturday for the main event. By 10 a.m., the flight line was packed—blankets and chairs arranged in careful rows, the serious photographers with their long lenses staked out near the runway threshold.

Commander Brian Kesselring, the Blue Angels' commanding officer and flight leader, spoke briefly at a VIP reception Friday evening. It's his second and final year leading the team.

"Coming home to Pensacola is different," Kesselring said. "These are our neighbors. Our kids go to school with their kids. The pressure is real."

The team's 45-minute demonstration is scheduled for 2 p.m. both days, weather permitting. Forecasts show partly cloudy skies with winds out of the southwest at 8 to 12 knots—nearly ideal conditions.

The Other Homecoming

The air show is the headline, but homecoming week sprawls across Pensacola. The National Naval Aviation Museum opened an exhibit Thursday on the history of the Blue Angels' aircraft, featuring a restored F11F Tiger, the jet the team flew from 1957 to 1969. The museum expects 15,000 visitors over the long weekend.

Downtown, the Pensacola Blue Wahoos are playing a four-game series against the Montgomery Biscuits, with Friday and Saturday games timed to end before the afternoon shows. The team is offering a "Flight Suit Friday" promotion—wear a flight suit, get half-price tickets.

Hotels across Escambia and Santa Rosa counties have been booked solid for months. Visit Pensacola, the region's tourism bureau, estimates the homecoming economic impact at $14.2 million, up from $12.8 million last year.

"This is our Super Bowl," said Darien Schaefer, Visit Pensacola's executive director. "Except it happens every year."

Looking Forward

The shuttle experiment will get its real verdict in the coming weeks, when city officials analyze ridership data, traffic flow, and rider surveys. If the numbers hold, Webb said, the program could become permanent.

"We're not declaring victory yet," he said. "But I drove Navy Boulevard this morning, and I didn't sit still for 45 minutes. That's something."

The Blue Angels take to the sky at 2 p.m. Sunday for the final demonstration of homecoming week. Gates open at 8 a.m. Shuttles begin running at 7:30 a.m. from all three downtown garages.

For those driving directly to the base, the official advice remains unchanged: leave early, bring patience, pack water. The traffic will be bad. It's homecoming. That's part of the deal.
